transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-10-11
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Alex Gomez (Redwood SE), Marcus Allen (Cascade - Head of Platform), Sofia Reyes (Cascade - Lead ML Eng), Evan Cole (Cascade - CTO)

Auto-generated summary (may contain errors): quick walkthrough of Redwood Optimise batching, kv cash (sic) vs prefix cache, cost model, and pilot scoping.

00:00 Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'll kick us off. Today Priya and Alex will run through Redwood Optimize recommendations for batching and prefix / KV cache and how you can lower token cost without blowing your p50 p99 latency. Marcus, Sofia, Evan, thanks for the context you sent over.
00:18 Marcus Allen: Yep thanks Jordan, quick note, our main constraints are p95 < 300ms for auth flows, most traffic is short prompts ~ 80-120 tokens but we have a tail of long conversations for dispute resolution. We also need everything to go through our VPC, and no raw logs leave the account.
00:36 Priya Nair: Got it, and that's a pretty common profile. We'll show a few batching approaches - synchronous small batches, adaptive batching, and request coalescing - and then dig into prefix (KV) cache. We'll also show some cost model math: tokens per request, hit rate assumptions, and how that maps to GPU utilization and cost.
01:05 Alex Gomez: Just to flag, sometimes the transcribe sees "Redwood Optimise" spelled differently, so ignore that in the notes :)
01:12 Sofia Reyes: ha, noted. Also curious how quantization plays into this because we've been testing 4-bit models in-house and want to know if Redwood supports that and how it changes economics.
01:23 Priya Nair: Yes we support quantized variants and we'll include a slide on perf delta; typically 4-bit quantization drops memory and increases throughput so cost per token goes down, but sometimes latency jitter increases slightly depending on kernel selection. We'll include the numbers.

03:02 Jordan Lee: Quick qualifying questions - what's your current stack for inference and what are the volumes?
03:09 Marcus Allen: We currently run a mix of managed endpoints (cloud provider) for bursty workloads and an internal Triton-based stack for sensitive flows. Rough numbers: peak 40 req/s, average 8 req/s, monthly tokens about 300M. We want to reduce hosted API costs but avoid building a full ops team to maintain Triton.
03:35 Priya Nair: That's helpful. With that profile the Optimize levers that matter are KV cache hit rate (for repeating prefixes), batching window tuning to avoid p95 regression, and model variant routing for cost-optimized tails.

05:00 (slide share) Priya Nair: First, batching strategies. Option A: small fixed batches with immediate dispatch (low latency, low batching efficiency). Option B: adaptive batching that waits up to X ms (you pick) for coalescing similar requests, higher throughput but adds a bounded delay. Option C: continuous batching on GPU worker where we aggregate inflight tokens - best throughput, needs more careful SLO tuning.
05:22 Marcus Allen: For our p95 < 300ms, what window would you recommend?
05:28 Priya Nair: For your token lengths, something like 10-20ms adaptive window gives you 20-30% batching efficiency without bumping p95 much. If you can tolerate 50-80ms, you get 2-3x efficiency but p95 will climb. We usually show the cost model with 15ms and 60ms cases.

07:10 Alex Gomez: Now KV vs prefix cache - couple ways folks cache: 
- KV cache (key-value kv cache) stores previous KV cache entries so for multi-turn or long contexts you avoid re-computing early layers.
- Prefix cache is a higher-level memoization: common prefixes (like templates, system prompts) get cached and returned quickly without model compute.

07:40 Sofia Reyes: So prefix cache is basically skipping compute for repeated opening text? We have a bunch of templated prompts across teams.
07:47 Priya Nair: Exactly. If 40% of your requests share a common 30-60 token prefix, prefix cache hit could dramatically cut tokens going to the model. KV cache helps for continuing conversations where only the delta is new. Both can be used together.

09:02 Jordan Lee: Example cost model slide. Baseline: no batching, no cache => cost X. Add 15ms batching => cost -25%. Add prefix cache 40% hit => cost -35% (cumulative). Add KV caching for multi-turn => another -10-20% depending on hit rate. The exact output depends on average tokens saved and hit rates.
09:34 Marcus Allen: Can you show the math for our numbers? Our average 100 tokens/request, 300M tokens/month baseline.
09:41 Priya Nair: Sure - quick calc: baseline GPU token cost approximated at $0.0003 per token (example, will send exact spreadsheet). At 300M tokens that's $90k/mo. With 25% batching gain => 225M effective tokens => $67.5k. With 40% prefix hit that reduces model tokens by 40% of requests (not tokens) - so effective tokens go down further to ~135M => $40.5k. Then KV cache on multi-turns might cut another 10-15% so final around $34k. These are illustrative; we'll send a sheet with your exact traffic for pro forma.
10:25 Evan Cole: That delta is huge, especially since we host some of this now. Biggest risk is latency - we can't have p95 spikes for auth paths.
10:33 Priya Nair: Totally. That's why we recommend hybrid routing: route strict auth flows to a low-latency dedicated pool with minimal batching and route background/chat flows to cost-optimized pools with higher batching and aggressive cache.

12:01 Alex Gomez: For private deployment we do a private control plane + VPC connectors so you can keep audit logs on premises, and we integrate with KMS/HSM - sometimes the transcriber writes H-M-S or K N S but it's KMS/HSM.
12:15 Marcus Allen: We need network diagrams and compliance docs for procurement.
12:19 Jordan Lee: We'll attach SOC2 pack and network diagram link in the follow up.

14:00 Priya Nair: Benchmarks - we recommend baseline microbenchmarks (latency p50/p95/p99), and a second round with production traffic replay. For production replay, we can run two configs in parallel: your current stack vs Redwood on identical input; measure cost per 1M requests and latency distributions.
14:30 Sofia Reyes: For the pilot, will you need us to scrub PII or can you run in our VPC?
14:36 Jordan Lee: We can run both. If you run in your VPC we don't take logs off-network; if you prefer hosted pilot we have redaction tooling and you can limit retention.

17:10 Priya Nair: Quick demo - here's the Optimize Console: per-route token breakdown, batching window slider, prefix cache hit rate graphs. The cache hit graph updates live and you can simulate X% hit to see cost estimates.
17:45 Marcus Allen: That simulator looked handy. Any typical hit rates you see in payments vertical?
17:52 Priya Nair: For payments with templated prompts we often see 30-50% prefix hit. KV cache hit varies - 10-25% depending on multi-turn rate.

20:05 Alex Gomez: Note about implementation: prefix cache is easiest to implement on the SDK side - tag requests with prefix keys or use our SDK call that computes canonical prefix tokens. KV caching requires store of kv blobs per session - we provide managed stores or you can supply your own in VPC.
20:26 Marcus Allen: If we use our own store, any specific throughput/consistency reqs?
20:30 Alex Gomez: We recommend a low-latency KV store (Redis or similar) with sub-5ms reads for hot paths; we batch fetches to avoid thundering herd. We'll include config examples.

23:10 Sofia Reyes: About quantization - we run 4-bit and saw some weird degredation on hallucination metrics. Does Redwood surface any perf-quality tradeoffs?
23:20 Priya Nair: Yes, Optimize has eval hooks; you can attach prompt suites and monitor quality regression per model/quantization profile. For customers with strict quality needs we recommend canarying quantized variants and keeping a higher-precision fallback route.

25:05 Jordan Lee: Objections & procurement - you'll need SOC2 and network diagrams, and for dedicated pools there's a commit term. Cascade is leaning toward a pilot first to validate cost/latency.
25:30 Evan Cole: Procurement will push for a short trial period without large commit. Is that possible?
25:37 Jordan Lee: Yes we support pilot contracts and proof-of-concept credits for trials. If you want dedicated capacity later we can discuss a short reserved term.

28:00 Q&A Marcus Allen: In the cost model sheet, can you include an example of 15ms vs 60ms batching window and corresponding p95 numbers?
28:10 Priya Nair: Absolutely. We'll run synthetic microbenchmarks and attach real-world numbers from similar customers.

30:05 Alex Gomez: One more technical note: kernel selection and compilation matter; our runtime picks kernels based on sequence length distribution. If you have lots of short prompts, different kernels optimize that path and reduce latency. We'll include recommended seq-length buckets.

33:40 Sofia Reyes: Action items recap?
33:45 Jordan Lee: Sure - Jordan will send cost-model spreadsheet and SOC2 docs. Priya will propose pilot dates and benchmark plan. Marcus will send sample traffic and retention/security constraints. We'll reconvene week of Oct 18 to review results.

34:05 Marcus Allen: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
34:10 Evan Cole: Appreciate the walkthrough.
34:14 Jordan Lee: Thanks - we'll follow up with the materials and schedule.

End of transcript. Note: There are occasional transcription errors (Optimise vs Optimize, KV cash, H-M-S instead of HSM) - please treat content as meeting notes not verbatim minutes.
